name: Mono (narrowed) reverb as a mixing and sound-design tool: narrow each 100%-wet reverb into a placeable 'pocket', pan pockets to separate parts, put a stereo ping-pong delay after the width stage so the pocket travels left-right, use the wet/dry mix as a distance control, filter the reverb tail post-reverb with an LFO-moved bandpass, and split dry left / mono reverb right for pseudo-stereo
goal: Clean up a crowded ambient or electronic mix and get new textures by making reverbs mono or narrow instead of wide. For each sound, decide what stays stereo (e.g. a wide atmos bed with high-end detail) and what becomes a pocket: narrow the reverb width (it does not have to be fully mono; side-reducing imagers sound better than fold-to-mono), then pan the pocket to its own spot and turn it down, since a centred or narrow reverb is more audible and needs less level. Put a ping-pong delay after the width utility (low feedback, lowpass in the feedback path) so the mono pocket moves left and right without washing the whole field. Treat the wet/dry mix as a distance knob: fully wet is far, fully dry is close, which is more obvious with mono reverb. Filter after the reverb with a bandpass moved back and forth (manually or by LFO), with the filter mix keeping some high end, to shape the tail as its own sound. For pseudo-stereo, put a mono reverb on a send, pan the dry sound fully left and the reverb fully right, then bus both through a driven resonant filter. A fully wet mono reverb on an atmos track, sidechained, becomes a wall of sound that sits behind the lead.

source.title: STOP Using Stereo Reverb (Do This Instead) (Dub Techno Tutorial Mixing)

prerequisites: DAW or Web Audio graph with reverb, stereo width/imager utility, panner, ping-pong delay and filters; in Web Audio: ConvolverNode → mono sum (ChannelMerger/Splitter or a mid-only gain) → StereoPannerNode → ping-pong delay pair (implementation note)

inputs.name: tracks
inputs.description: Parts competing for space (atmos, steps, plucks, chords)

outputs.name: stereo_map
outputs.description: Per-track: stays stereo or pocket, width, pan, reverb level

outputs.name: pocket_fx_chains
outputs.description: Reverb → width → pan → ping-pong delay → post filter chains

constraints: Original synthesis recipe; not affiliated with any vendor named in the source. Recreate in browser/Web Audio (Polyrhythm Studio) or any hybrid synth with comparable modules; no presets, banks or samples copied.
Narrowing can be partial: keep a sound slightly wider if it serves the part, as long as it reads as one source.
Prefer side-reducing width control over hard mono summing to avoid phase cancellation.
If vocals are the main element, the presenter suggests stereo reverb on them; mono reverb suits chops, drums, claps and hats.
No numbers were given apart from 100% wet and full-left/full-right pans. Set the rest by ear. Plugin names not needed.

steps.action: Solo through the parts and decide which stays stereo (e.g. an atmos bed with high-end detail through a moving notch filter into a 100% wet reverb) and which become mono/narrow pockets.
steps.expect: A list of stereo vs pocket tracks

steps.action: For a pocket track, set its reverb 100% wet (on the insert) and narrow its width with a side-reducing imager or width utility, partly or fully.
steps.expect: The reverb becomes a focused, one-dimensional pocket

steps.action: Pan each pocket to its own spot (e.g. short step pocket right, layered second step slightly wider and left, main part centre) and turn levels down: narrow reverbs are more audible, so they need less.
steps.expect: Parts stop fighting; the mix gets clearer at lower levels

steps.action: Put the ping-pong delay after the width stage, with low feedback and a lowpass on the feedback, so the mono pocket is carried left and right.
steps.expect: A narrow sound that still moves across the stereo field

steps.action: Use the reverb mix as a distance control: fully wet = far behind, fully dry = right in front. Shave highs for extra depth.
Place a bandpass filter after the reverb and move it back and forth by hand or with an LFO; use the filter's mix to keep some high end. Post-reverb filtering shapes the tail as its own sound.
steps.expect: The reverb shadow becomes a moving, organic texture

steps.action: Pseudo-stereo: send the sound to a mono reverb return, pan the dry sound hard left and the reverb hard right, then route both to a bus with a driven, resonant filter (cut lows, shorten the reverb, add movement).
steps.expect: Two mono sources that together sound wide

steps.action: For a background wall: put a fully wet mono reverb on the atmos track and sidechain it to the lead or kick so it ducks out of the way.
steps.expect: A dense bed that sits behind the main part

verification: After narrowing, the pocket can be moved with the pan control and is heard as one spot.
With the delay placed after the width utility, repeats alternate left and right while the reverb itself stays narrow.
Sweeping the reverb mix from dry to wet makes the source move audibly from front to back.
The dry-left / reverb-right pair sounds wider than either part alone, while each side stays a single focused source.
